en: Majjhima Nikāya 28:
The Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus!”
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

“Friends, just as all the various footprints of forest animals are encompassed within the footprint of an elephant, and the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost among them by virtue of its size;”
In the same way, friends, whatever wholesome states there are, they are all included within the Four Noble Truths.
Within which four?
In the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering?

Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not to obtain what one desires is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
And what, friends, are the five aggregates of clinging?

They are as follows: the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.
And what, friends, is the form aggregate subject to clinging?
It is the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
And what, friends, are the four great elements?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
And what, friends, is the earth element?
The earth element may be internal or external.
And what, friends, is the internal earth element?
Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, solid, harsh, and clung-to; that is to say:
Head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver,
midriff, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces, or whatever else there is internally,
belonging to oneself, that is hard, solid, and clung-to.
This, friends, is called the internal earth element.
Now, both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element.
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus it should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and detaches the mind from the earth element.
There comes a time, friends, when the external water element is disturbed;
at that time, the external earth element disappears.
For even in that external earth element, which is so vast, impermanence is discerned; the nature of destruction is discerned; the nature of vanishing is discerned; the nature of change is discerned.
What then of this body, consisting of mere foam, seized by craving, regarding which one might think "I" or "mine" or "I am"? Indeed, in this case, such thoughts do not arise at all.
And if, friends, others abuse, revile, irritate, or harass that bhikkhu, he understands thus:
‘This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me.
And it is dependent, not independent.
Dependent on what?’

“Dependent on contact. He sees that contact is impermanent; he sees that feeling is impermanent; he sees that perception is impermanent; he sees that volitional formations are impermanent; he sees that consciousness is impermanent.
His mind leaps forward toward the elements as its object, gains confidence in them, becomes settled in them, and resolves upon them.
If others treat that bhikkhu with what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable—
even by means of contact with the hand, contact with clods of earth, contact with sticks, or contact with weapons—
he understands thus:
“This body is such that upon it the touch of hands occurs, the touch of clods occurs, the touch of sticks occurs, and the touch of weapons occurs.
And this was said by the Blessed One in the *Kakacūpama-sutta* (The Simile of the Saw):
‘Monks, even if bandits with a two-handled saw were to sever your limbs and appendages one by one, whoever should allow their mind to become corrupted thereby would not be following my instruction.’”
“Indeed, my energy shall be aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness shall be established and unconfused; my body shall be tranquil and unagitated; my mind shall be concentrated and one-pointed.

Let there now be contact with my body by hand, let there be contact with clods of earth, let there be contact with sticks, and let there be contact with weapons. For this is how the teaching of the Buddhas is practiced.”

If, friends, while that bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, thus recollecting the Dhamma, and thus recollecting the Saṅgha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established, he is stirred by that and experiences a sense of spiritual urgency:
"It is a loss for me indeed! It is no gain for me! It is ill-gained by me indeed! It is no good gain for me!"
‘When I thus recollect the Buddha, thus recollect the Dhamma, and thus recollect the Saṅgha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in me.

Just as, friends, a daughter-in-law is stirred and experiences a sense of urgency upon seeing her father-in-law, even so, friends, when that bhikkhu thus recollects the Buddha, thus recollects the Dhamma... [and thus recollects the Saṅgha]...”
As he thus recollects the Saṅgha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established; stirred by that, he experiences a sense of spiritual urgency:

"It is a loss for me, truly a loss for me! It is ill-gained for me, truly ill-gained for me, that as I thus recollect the Buddha, thus recollect the Dhamma, and thus recollect the Saṅgha, equanimity..."
‘It does not settle on the wholesome.
If, friends, as that bhikkhu thus recollects the Buddha, thus recollects the Dhamma, and thus recollects the Saṅgha, equanimity supported by the wholesome settles in him, he is satisfied with that.
To this extent, friends, much has been done by that bhikkhu.”
And what, friends, is the water element?
The water element may be internal or it may be external.
And what, friends, is the internal water element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water or watery,

and is clung-to, namely: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water or watery and is clung-to— this, friends,
is called the internal water element.
Now, both the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element.
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and detaches the mind from the water element.
"There comes a time, friends, when the external water element becomes disturbed.
It sweeps away villages, it sweeps away towns, it sweeps away cities, it sweeps away districts, and it sweeps away the regions of the countryside.
There comes a time, friends, when the waters in the great ocean recede by a hundred leagues, even by two hundred leagues."
The waters recede; the waters recede even by three hundred yojanas, they recede even by four hundred yojanas,
they recede even by five hundred yojanas, they recede even by six hundred yojanas,
and they recede even by seven hundred yojanas.
"There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands at the height of seven palm trees;
it stands at the height of six palm trees; it stands at the height of five palm trees; it stands at the height of four palm trees; it stands at the height of three palm trees;
it stands at the height of two palm trees; and it stands at the height of one palm tree."

"There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands at the height of seven fathoms; it stands at six fathoms, five fathoms, four fathoms, three fathoms, two fathoms, and even at the height of one fathom."
"There is, friends, a time when the water in the great ocean stands at the height of half a man, or at the height of the waist, or at the height of the knees, or at the height of the ankles.
There is, friends, a time when there is not even enough water in the great ocean to wet a finger-joint."

For even in this external water element, so vast and extensive, impermanence will be discerned; the nature of decay will be discerned; the nature of vanishing will be discerned; the nature of change will be discerned.
What then of this body, a mere trifle, gripped by craving—how could one think of it as "I," or "mine," or "I am"? Thus, indeed, there is no such thing here... [as before]...

If, friends, while that bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, thus recollecting the Dhamma, and thus recollecting the Saṅgha, equanimity supported by the wholesome becomes established, he is satisfied with that.
To this extent, friends, much has been done by that bhikkhu.
And what, friends, is the fire element?
The fire element may be internal, and it may be external.
And what, friends, is the internal fire element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire or of the nature of fire, and is clung to; that is to say:
That by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed,
and tasted is properly digested, or whatever else internally and personally is fire, fiery, and clung-to— this, friends, is called the internal fire element.
Now, both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element.
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and detaches the mind from the fire element.
"There comes a time, friends, when the external fire element becomes disturbed.
It burns villages, it burns towns, it burns cities, it burns districts, and it burns even parts of districts.
Having reached the edge of greenery, or the edge of a road, or the edge of rocks, or the edge of water, or a delightful stretch of ground, it goes out for lack of fuel."
"There comes a time, friends, when they seek fire even with a cock’s feather or a piece of sinew.
For even that external fire-element, so vast, is seen to be subject to impermanence, subject to exhaustion, subject to vanishing, and subject to change.
How much more so this body, a mere trifle, gripped by craving—how could it be thought of as 'I', or 'mine', or 'I am'?"

Then, indeed, there is no more thinking in him regarding this... [as before] ...If, friends, as that bhikkhu thus recollects the Buddha, thus recollects the Dhamma, and thus recollects the Saṅgha, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established in him, he is satisfied by that.
To this extent, friends, much has been done by that bhikkhu.
And what, friends, is the air element?
The air element may be internal or it may be external.
And what, friends, is the internal air element?
Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air or airy, and is clung-to, namely: winds that move upward,
winds that move downward, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs and members, inhalation and exhalation, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself,
is air or airy and is clung-to— this, friends, is called the internal air element.
Whatever internal air element there is, and whatever external air element there is—that is simply the air element.
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and detaches the mind from the air element.
"There comes a time, friends, when the external wind element becomes disturbed.
It sweeps away villages, it sweeps away towns, it sweeps away cities, it sweeps away districts, and it sweeps away even parts of districts.
There comes a time, friends, in the last month of summer, when people seek the wind even with palm-leaf fans or whisks, and do not even wish for grasses at the water's edge."
For even in that external air element, so vast in extent, impermanence is evident, the nature of exhaustion is evident, the nature of vanishing is evident, and the nature of change is evident.

How much more so, then, for this body, which is but a handful in size and gripped by craving—how could one think of it as ‘I,’ or ‘mine,’ or ‘I am’? Indeed, in this regard, such a thought does not arise at all.
And if, friends, others abuse, revile, threaten, or harass that bhikkhu...
Thus he understands: "This painful feeling born of ear-contact has indeed arisen in me;
and it has arisen dependently, not independently.
Dependent upon what?"

Dependent on contact. He sees that contact too is impermanent; he sees that feeling is impermanent; he sees that perception is impermanent; he sees that formations are impermanent; he sees that consciousness is impermanent.
His mind leaps forward toward the elements as its object, becomes confident, settles, and resolves upon it.

If others treat that bhikkhu with what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable—even with the touch of a hand, the touch of a clod, the touch of a staff, or the touch of a sword—he understands thus:
“This body is of such a nature that it is subject to the touch of a hand, the touch of a clod, the touch of a staff, and the touch of a sword.”

Furthermore, this was said by the Blessed One in the *Kakacūpama-sutta* (The Simile of the Saw): “Bhikkhus, even if bandits with saws having teeth on both sides were to sever your limbs and appendages one by one, if you should harbor an evil thought in that regard, you would not be following my instruction.
Indeed, my energy shall be aroused and unflagging; my mindfulness shall be established and unconfused; my body shall be tranquil and unagitated; and my mind shall be concentrated and one-pointed.

"Let there now be contact with the hand upon this body; let there be contact with clods of earth; let there be contact with sticks; let there be contact with weapons. For here the teaching of the Buddhas is being practiced.

If, friend, as that bhikkhu thus recollects the Buddha, thus recollects the Dhamma, and thus recollects the Saṅgha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established, he becomes stirred by that, he experiences a sense of spiritual urgency:
"It is indeed a loss for me, truly not a gain for me;

it is ill-gained by me, truly not well-gained by me, that while I am thus recollecting the Buddha, thus recollecting the Dhamma, and thus recollecting the Saṅgha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established.
It is just as if, friends, a daughter-in-law, upon seeing her father-in-law, is stirred and experiences a sense of urgency.

In the same way, friends, if while a bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, thus recollecting the Dhamma, and thus recollecting the Saṅgha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established, he is stirred by that and experiences a sense of urgency:
"It is a loss for me indeed! It is no gain for me! It is ill-gained by me indeed! It is no good gain for me!"
‘When I thus recollect the Buddha, thus recollect the Dhamma, and thus recollect the Saṅgha, equanimity supported by the wholesome does not become established.

If, friends, when that bhikkhu thus recollects the Buddha, thus recollects the Dhamma, and thus recollects the Saṅgha, equanimity supported by the wholesome becomes established, he is satisfied with that.
To this extent, friends, much has been done by that bhikkhu.”
Just as, friends, space enclosed by wood, creepers, grass, and clay comes to be designated as a "house," so too,
friends, space enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin comes to be designated as "form."

Friends, if the internal eye is intact, but external forms do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding act of attention, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness does not occur.

Friends, if the internal eye is intact and external forms come into its range, but there is no corresponding act of attention, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness does not occur.

But when, friends, the internal eye is unimpaired and external forms come into its range, and there is the corresponding application of attention, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness occurs.
Whatever form belongs to one who is thus constituted, that is included within the aggregate of clinging to form;

whatever feeling belongs to one who is thus constituted, that is included within the aggregate of clinging to feeling; whatever perception belongs to one who is thus constituted, that is included within the aggregate of clinging to perception.
It is included; those formations belonging to one who has become thus are included in the aggregate of clinging to formations;
that consciousness belonging to one who has become thus is included in the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
He understands thus:
‘For indeed, it is said that there is this collection, this meeting, this combination of these five aggregates of clinging.
And this was said by the Blessed One:
“He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma;’”’
“He who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.
Now, these five aggregates of clinging are dependently arisen.
Whatever desire, attachment, inclination, and craving there is for these five aggregates of clinging—that is the origin of suffering.
‘The removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for these five aggregates of clinging—that is the cessation of suffering.
To this extent, friend, much has been done by a bhikkhu.
Furthermore, friend, if the internal ear is unimpaired... [and so on].
The nose is unimpaired;
the tongue is unimpaired;
the body is unimpaired.

When the internal mind is intact, but external phenomena do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding act of attention, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness does not occur.

Furthermore, friends, when the internal mind is intact and external phenomena come into its range, but there is no corresponding act of attention, then the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness does not occur.

But when, friends, the internal mind is intact, external phenomena come into its range, and there is the corresponding attention, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness.
Whatever form belongs to one who is thus constituted, that is included within the aggregate of clinging to form;

whatever feeling belongs to one who is thus constituted, that is included within the aggregate of clinging to feeling; whatever perception belongs to one who is thus constituted, that is included within the aggregate of clinging to perception.
It is included; those formations belonging to one who has become thus are included in the aggregate of clinging to formations;
that consciousness belonging to one who has become thus is included in the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
He understands thus:
‘For indeed, it is said that there is this gathering, this coming together, this combination of these five aggregates of clinging.
And this has been said by the Blessed One:
“He who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma;’”’
“He who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.
Now, these five aggregates of clinging are dependently arisen.
Whatever desire, attachment, inclination, and clinging there is toward these five aggregates of clinging—that is the origin of suffering.
“The subduing of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for these five aggregates of clinging—that is the cessation of suffering.
To this extent, friend, much has been done by a bhikkhu.
This is what the Venerable Sāriputta said.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta’s words.
The Great Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint, the eighth, is finished.
